content: This document provides interim guidance for countries on laboratory testing strategies and considerations for suspected cases of severe acute hepatitis of unknown etiology in children. It categorizes diagnostic tests into three groups to aid prioritization: 1. Case Definition Diagnostics: These are tests required to meet the current WHO case definition for severe acute hepatitis of unknown etiology. 2. Additional Diagnostics: These tests aim to exclude other well-recognized causes of severe acute hepatitis in children. 3. Investigative Diagnostics: These are tests designed to identify potential etiologies. Early collection of key specimens is strongly recommended, ideally as soon as possible after symptom onset. Whole blood is the preferred specimen type, but other specimens such as serum, plasma, throat swabs, stool, or urine are also encouraged. Liver biopsies should only be performed if clinically necessary and feasible. All specimens must be stored under appropriate conditions to preserve their integrity. Assessment of other potential etiological factors, including infectious agents, environmental exposures (toxins, medications), metabolic hereditary conditions, or autoimmune disorders, should be conducted in consultation with a pediatric hepatologist. A comprehensive set of investigative diagnostics may include testing for a variety of viruses, bacteria, parasites, and fungi. This list should be adapted based on the country and region, particularly considering endemic infectious diseases. If local laboratory capacity is limited, specimens should be stored and referred to regional or global laboratories for further testing. Any positive specimens should also be stored for additional testing or follow-up investigations. Background Cases of severe acute hepatitis of unknown etiology in children continue to be reported across multiple countries, with the majority of cases currently originating from the WHO European Region. Probable cases and cases pending classification have also been reported in the Americas, Western Pacific, South-East Asia, and Eastern Mediterranean regions. Enhanced case-finding activities are expected to result in more reported cases in the coming weeks. In some countries, the number of cases exceeds the usual low background rates of severe acute hepatitis of unknown etiology in children. The five hepatitis viruses (A, B, C, D, and E) that typically account for most hepatitis cases worldwide have tested negative in these recent cases. While the cause or causes remain unknown, investigations into potential known or unknown etiologies are ongoing. These investigations include infectious (bacterial, fungal, parasitic, and virological) and non-infectious agents, environmental exposures (toxins or certain medicines), autoimmune disorders, and metabolic hereditary conditions. To date, no clear risk factors or causes have been identified. Testing Indications Given the unknown etiology, testing decisions should be based on clinical assessment and the need to rule out potential known causes of severe acute hepatitis in children. Good clinical practice principles should guide clinicians and healthcare workers in supporting children presenting with signs and symptoms of severe acute hepatitis. WHO recommends that clinicians, epidemiologists, and laboratory scientists consult the WHO case definition to determine which cases require reporting and potential further investigation. The case definitions are regularly reviewed and updated as new information becomes available. Case Definition The current WHO working case definitions are as follows: Confirmed: Not applicable at present. Probable: A person presenting with acute hepatitis (non-hepatitis A-E) with serum transaminase levels >500 IU/L (AST or ALT), aged 16 years or younger, since October 2021. Epi-linked: A person presenting with acute hepatitis (non-hepatitis A-E) of any age who is a close contact of a probable case since October 2021. Cases with other explanations for their clinical presentation are excluded. If hepatitis A-E serology results are pending but other criteria are met, these cases can be reported and classified as pending classification. Diagnostic Testing To identify probable cases of severe acute hepatitis of unknown etiology in children, the following diagnostic tests should be performed: Assessment of Severity: Aspartate transaminase (AST) and/or alanine transaminase (ALT) levels. Hepatitis Virus Testing: Hepatitis A, B, C, and E viruses. Hepatitis D testing is only required if hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) is positive to establish co-infection. Specimen Collection, Storage, and Transport A variety of specimens should be collected from individuals meeting the case definition as soon as possible after symptom onset. Periodic testing should also be considered. Specimens should be prioritized for collection even if local testing capacity is unavailable, to meet the case definition and support investigations into the etiology. Specimens may be referred to national, regional, or global laboratories when local capacity is limited. Specimens should be collected sequentially, including at symptom onset, during clinical deterioration or changes in condition, prior to and following treatment, and during convalescence. Proper storage of samples is critical for future testing and investigations. Specimens collected for research purposes must adhere to local and national ethical guidelines, including informed consent. Specimen Types and Storage Recommendations Whole Blood: Preferred specimen type; store at 2-8°C if ≤3 days, or at -20°C for >3 days. Serum: Store at 2-8°C if ≤7 days, or at -20°C for >7 days. Plasma: Store at 2-8°C if ≤3 days, or at -20°C for >3 days. Respiratory Specimens: Store at 2-8°C if ≤3 days, or at -20°C for >3 days. Stool/Rectal Swab: Store at 2-8°C if ≤3 days, or at -20°C for >3 days. Urine: Store at 2-8°C if ≤3 days, or at -20°C for >3 days. Liver Tissue: Store at 2-8°C if ≤3 days, or at -20°C for >3 days. For histopathology, use 10% buffered formaldehyde at room temperature. Specimens stored for future testing should ideally be kept at -80°C. Any positive specimens should be stored for further testing and follow-up investigations. Investigative Diagnostics If case definition diagnostic tests are negative, further investigations into differential diagnoses can begin. These may include comprehensive screening for viral and non-viral infections, toxicology, and specialized investigations such as metagenomics. Metagenomics involves sequencing and analyzing all genetic material in a specimen to identify both known and unknown pathogens. It is recommended for investigative purposes when diagnostic tests are inconclusive. Ethical Considerations Ethical considerations must be taken into account when conducting testing for investigative or research purposes rather than diagnostic or clinical purposes. National and regional contexts, such as varying infectious disease pathogens, should also be considered. Testing Strategy The current case definition is exclusive, requiring the exclusion of viral hepatitis A, B, C, and E as underlying causes and a measure of hepatitis severity (AST or ALT testing). However, other well-recognized causes of severe acute hepatitis in children should also be prioritized as part of the ongoing clinical work-up. Initial diagnostic tests should be prioritized to ensure that any possible case meets the case definition. Once a probable case is identified, additional investigative diagnostics may be considered. The relevance and feasibility of these tests will vary by region and country capacity. Facilities with limited laboratory capacity or resources should prioritize specimen collection and storage for future or referral testing.
